description: We are SOMONIX, a team from Tajikistan who love space, games and building things that really work. Our skills: front-end (React, three.js), back-end and game logic (TypeScript, physics simulation), UI/UX, testing and deployment. We built GO / NO-GO: Mission Control, a game where you design and fly a real satellite mission.
summary: GO / NO-GO: Mission Control is a browser game where players design, launch and operate a complete satellite mission. A customer asks for a job, such as finding wildfires, watching hurricanes or mapping a city. The player builds the satellite from 12 parts (instrument, power, battery, radio, memory, computer and more), chooses a rocket, an orbit and ground stations, then flies the mission over a 3D Earth made from NASA imagery. A physics engine decides the outcome: Earth's shadow, air drag, radio speed, orbit tilt, mass and budget are all computed. When a mission fails, the report marks each requirement GO or NO-GO, explains why in plain words and opens the part to change. Six missions go from easy to hard, each teaching one trade-off. A crew mode lets up to four players share mission-control roles and launch only when everyone votes GO. This addresses the challenge directly. Students rarely experience a whole mission, so trade-offs stay abstract. Our game makes them visible, playable and memorable: try, fail, understand why, fly again.
details:
GO / NO-GO: Mission Control is a browser game that lets players run a complete satellite mission, from the customer's request to operations in orbit. Each mission starts with a brief from a customer. The Forest Fire Service needs 10 fire photos over 3 years, climate scientists need photos of glaciers at 75° N, a weather service must watch hurricanes nonstop. The player builds the satellite from 12 parts: instrument, body, solar panels, battery, antenna, memory, computer, debris shield, thruster, rocket, orbit and ground stations. Live gauges show mass, power, battery in Earth's shadow and budget, and the launch is blocked if the rocket can't lift the satellite, can't reach the orbit, or the cost tops the budget. After a 3D launch, the player flies the mission over a NASA Earth: they photograph targets, send data home over ground stations, and survive Earth's shadow, space junk and solar storms.

Every number comes from a mission engine we wrote in TypeScript. It computes the orbital period, the share of each orbit spent in Earth's shadow, passes over ground stations, orbit lifetime from air drag, and the power, data, mass and cost budgets. The flight feels like an arcade game, but its rules come from the engine: if the battery dies in the game, the energy budget really doesn't close. At the end, the report marks each requirement GO or NO-GO, explains every failure in plain words, such as the battery running flat in Earth's shadow, and opens the part to change. Stars reward meeting and beating the goal. After a win, a card shows the real NASA mission that does the same job: FIRMS, ICESat-2, GOES, the Van Allen Probes or Landsat. In crew mode, 2 to 4 players join from their own phones or laptops and take the roles of flight director, spacecraft engineer, mission scientist and communications. Each role owns its parts, and the satellite launches only when every role votes GO.

Students usually learn orbits, rockets and spacecraft as separate topics. Our game shows how they interact: a sharper camera means more mass, more power, bigger files and a higher cost. Six missions go from easy to hard, and each one teaches a single trade-off: delivering data, surviving Earth's shadow, choosing the orbit's tilt, choosing the orbit itself, coping with radiation, and finally managing everything on a tight budget. Failure is safe and explained, so players learn by trying again. The game is free, runs in any browser, needs no account and works for ages 10 and up. We want classrooms and clubs anywhere to experience real mission design, not just read about it.

We built the game with TypeScript and React 19. The 3D scenes use three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei, and Vite builds the project. Crew mode runs on a Node.js server with socket.io, and the sound is synthesized live with the Web Audio API, so there are no audio files. We tested with Vitest and with a bot that plays every mission in the browser through Playwright, and the game is hosted behind a Caddy web server. We used NASA's Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery for the Earth. CubeSat 101, the Mission Design Lab, Mission Viz and Design and Develop Science Missions shaped the rules. No special hardware is needed: the game runs on any phone or laptop.

The game is creative in how it teaches. Each mission is a customer story, and the starter satellite is designed to fail in a way that teaches something. The GO / NO-GO idea runs through the whole game, from the report to the crew's launch vote, just like a real launch poll. The 3D satellite is built from the player's exact parts, and every win connects to a real NASA mission.

We weighed scientific honesty against simplicity for a 10-year-old. We made sure there is more than one winning design. Mission balance is checked automatically, so every reference design wins and every starter satellite fails. We built for phones first, with a portrait layout, touch controls and a 2D fallback for devices without WebGL. We also respected NASA's rules on its brand, so the game uses no NASA logos and no photos of people.
